decision.location: Results (Fig. 8B replicon RNA synthesis comparison, chunk 54, chars 49501-50601)
decision.reason: In Results (Fig. 8B, chunk 54), Isken et al. electroporate bicistronic NS2-5B/NCP7 WT and NS2-5B/CP7 WT reporter replicons into naive MDBK, DNAJC14-KO, and rescue cells, measure Renilla luciferase RNA replication at 2, 24, and 48 hpe, and explicitly compare their new observation—that NS2-5B/NCP7 WT exhibits lower replication efficiency than NS2-5B/CP7 WT in naive MDBK cells at 24 and 48 hpe—as being 'in line with the lower RNA replication efficiency known for NCP7 infections than CP7 infections (14)'. Although broader background statements jointly cite references 14 and 15 for temporal regulation of NS2-3 cleavage (chunks 10, 66) and local full texts of 2004/2005 are unavailable, the current paper itself distinguishes the two published findings: Lackner et al. (2004, ref 14, 'Temporal modulation of an autoprotease is crucial for replication and pathogenicity of an RNA virus', DOI 10.1128/JVI.78.19.10765-10775.2004) established the viral NS2 autoprotease temporal modulation and the lower NCP7-versus-CP7 RNA replication efficiency and biotype switch (chunks 54, 72), whereas shipped row 113 (Lackner et al., 2005, ref 15, 'Persistence of Bovine Viral Diarrhea Virus Is Determined by a Cellular Cofactor of a Viral Autoprotease', DOI 10.1128/jvi.79.15.9746-9755.2005) identified the limiting host cofactor DNAJC14/Jiv90 and incomplete steady-state cleavage under Jiv90 overexpression (chunks 7, 11, 12, 42). Because Fig. 8B empirically retests and directly compares against the separately attributable 2004 NCP7-versus-CP7 RNA replication efficiency finding (14), target 0 is a valid missing replication row.

decision.location: Discussion (paragraph 3, chunk 28, chars 22602-23702); see also Introduction (chunks 4, 8)
decision.quote: This study confirms several patterns that have emerged in previous work ( Bergelson & Swingley, 2012 , 2013b ; Parise & Csibra, 2012 ; Tincoff & Jusczyk, 1999 , 2012 ). Namely, we find further evidence, with a new sample of infants and a new set of item pairs, that 6-9 month olds understand words. Not unexpectedly, this ability increases with age, but perhaps less expectedly the rate with which it increases is non-linear. This is the third study that finds evidence of a boost in performance around 13-14 months, independent of word type ( Bergelson & Swingley, 2012 , 2013b ). We find three possible explanations for this boost viable. First, this is around the time that infants begin talking ( Dale & Fenson, 1996 ), which may increase their metalinguistic awareness, or understanding of words as community-wide symbols in a way that boosts comprehension . Second, this is just before the time that infants begin to show basic syntactic knowledge, and this in turn may help them use the distribution of arguments in the sentence to listen more predictively ( Jin & Fisher, 2014 ). decision.reason: The Discussion (chunk 28) collectively states that this study 'confirms several patterns that have emerged in previous work (Bergelson & Swingley, 2012, 2013b; Parise & Csibra, 2012; Tincoff & Jusczyk, 1999, 2012)' by providing further evidence that 6-9-month-olds understand words. However, per infant_originals_0106 and Introduction chunk 4, Parise & Csibra (2012, DOI 10.1177/0956797612438734) tested 28 9-month-old Hungarian infants in an ERP paradigm measuring the N400 mismatch effect when a single static object revealed after a delay was incongruent with a common object label spoken live by the mother versus an experimenter (finding an N400 mismatch for maternal speech only). While measurement modality alone does not exclude conceptual replication, the current study neither tests ERP/N400 mismatch nor contrasts maternal with unfamiliar speakers; rather, as Introduction chunk 8 explicitly defines the study's replication target, 'this study set out to replicate the basic finding of previous work, i.e. that young infants understand common nouns, while also extending the range of the words tested, and their format of presentation' using paired competing videos and eye-gaze. That behavioural common-noun comprehension finding in 6-9-month-olds is already directly represented by the closer behavioural eye-tracking studies in the same chain—shipped row 391 (Bergelson & Swingley, 2012) and approved sibling target 4 (Tincoff & Jusczyk, 2012)—making a separate row for Parise & Csibra (2012) unwarranted.

decision.location: Introduction (final paragraph, chunk 8, chars 6704-7586); see also Discussion (chunk 28)
decision.quote:
The present research examined early comprehension of words that were instantiated as competing video stimuli. We presented 6–16-month-old infants with a broad set of common words, such as “dog” and “car” (see Table 1 ). The words we tested had some overlap with previous work, but only one pair of nouns (hand-feet) had been tested before with young infants, as either still images or video clips ( Tincoff & Jusczyk, 2012 ). We also included two pairs of verbs, one of which was tested in Bergelson & Swingley (2013b) . Thus, this study set out to replicate the basic finding of previous work, i.e. that young infants understand common nouns, while also extending the range of the words tested, and their format of presentation. The present study also extends previous findings in its methods, utilizing a varied series of video stimuli over twelve trials.

decision.reason: Although Discussion chunk 28 includes Tincoff & Jusczyk (1999, DOI 10.1111/1467-9280.00127) in the five-study group citation for the broad pattern that 6-9-month-olds understand words, the primary abstract (infant_originals_0106) and Introduction chunk 5 show that Tincoff & Jusczyk (1999) specifically tested 6-month-olds' comprehension of the proper names 'Mommy' and 'Daddy' using videos of the infant's own parents versus unfamiliar parents (demonstrating parent-specific attachment-figure recognition rather than generic category comprehension). The present study tests six yoked pairs of common nouns and verbs (bottle-car, dog-bear, drink-kiss, hand-feet, hug-eat, juice-ball; chunk 11) and no proper names or parent videos. Crucially, when defining the study's empirical overlap and replication design in Introduction chunk 8 and Materials chunk 11, the authors explicitly link the paired-video common-noun retest to the closer follow-up paper Tincoff & Jusczyk (2012) ('only one pair of nouns (hand-feet) had been tested before with young infants, as either still images or video clips (Tincoff & Jusczyk, 2012)'), along with Bergelson & Swingley (2012, shipped row 391) and Bergelson & Swingley (2013b, target 1). Thus, the empirical retest in the Tincoff & Jusczyk paired-video lineage is captured by the closer 2012 common-noun study (target 4) and shipped row 391, not the 1999 Mommy/Daddy study.
